blocks.content: Both attach external storage to a container, but they solve different problems: volumes are Docker-managed and portable, bind mounts are host-specific and directly controllable. Knowing which one fits a given situation is a genuinely practical, frequently asked question.

A volume's actual location on disk is entirely Docker's decision, you interact with it only by name. A bind mount is the opposite, you specify the exact host path yourself, Docker has no say in where it actually lives.

blocks.alt: Docker decides for volumes, you decide for bind mounts

blocks.content: A named volume works identically regardless of which machine Docker happens to be running on, the same docker run -v myvolume:/data command works whether it is your laptop or a production server. A bind mount pointing at a specific host path is inherently tied to that one machine's filesystem layout.

blocks.alt: Volumes travel with your commands, bind mounts do not

blocks.content: {"headers":["","Named Volume","Bind Mount"],"rows":[["Who chooses the storage location","Docker","You, an exact host path"],["Portable across different hosts","Yes","No, tied to that host's paths"],["Good fit for","Production data, databases","Local development, live code reload"],["Managed with","docker volume commands","Ordinary host filesystem tools"]]}

The practical rule of thumb: use a named volume for anything you want Docker to manage and that needs to work the same way across different machines, most obviously production application data. Use a bind mount when you specifically need direct, live access to files on your own host, most obviously local development.

blocks.alt: Production data reaches for a volume, live dev reaches for a bind mount

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Volumes are Docker-managed and portable across hosts, bind mounts give you direct control over an exact host path but are tied to that host.
Reach for a volume for production, host-independent data, reach for a bind mount for local development workflows like live code reload.
